entries.21402c16c0d9ac40a933a08f51434561f5e8bd14: <div sID="gen32323" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="2Thess.3" sID="2Thess.3"/> <div eID="gen32323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32324" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32325" type="x-p"/> In the close of the foregoing chapter, the apostle had prayed earnestly for the Thessalonians, and now he desires their prayers, encouraging them to trust in God, to which he subjoins another petition for them, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.1-2Thess.3.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. He then proceeds to give them commands and directions for correcting some things he was informed were amiss among them (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.6-2Thess.3.15">ver. 6-15</reference>) and concludes with benedictions and prayers, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.16-2Thess.3.18">ver. 16-18</reference>.
entries.c276ebd35326837a4a7f1a906e16c6cca97edf5f: <div eID="gen32325" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32324" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Pious Request. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 52.)</title> <div sID="gen32326" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have <hi type="italic">free</hi> course, and be glorified, even as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> with you: <hi type="super">2</hi> And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all <hi type="italic">men</hi> have not faith. 3 But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep <hi type="italic">you</hi> from evil. <hi type="super">4</hi> And we have confidence in the Lord touching you, that ye both do and will do the things which we command you. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patient waiting for Christ. <div eID="gen32326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32327" type="x-p"/> In these words observe, <div eID="gen32327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32328" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle desires the prayers of his friends: <hi type="italic">Finally, brethren, pray for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.1">v. 1</reference>. He always remembered them in his prayers, and would not have them forget him and his fellow-labourers, but bear them on their hearts at the throne of grace. Note, 1. This is one way by which the communion of saints is kept us, not only by their praying together, or with one another, but by their praying for one another when they are absent one from another. And thus those who are at great distance may meet together at the throne of grace; and thus those who are not capable of doing or receiving any other kindness may yet this way do and receive real and very great kindness. 2. It is the duty of people to pray for their ministers; and not only for their own pastors, but also for all good and faithful ministers. And, 3. Ministers need, and therefore should desire, the prayers of their people. How remarkable is the humility, and how engaging the example, of this great apostle, who was so mighty in prayer himself, and yet despised not the prayers of the meanest Christian, but desired an interest in them. Observe, further, what they are desired and directed to pray for; namely, (1.) For the success of the gospel ministry: <hi type="italic">That the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.1">v. 1</reference>. This was the great thing that Paul was most solicitous about. He was more solicitous that God's name might be sanctified, his kingdom advanced, and his will done, than he was about his own daily bread. He desired that the word of the Lord might run (so it is in the original), that it might get ground, that the interest of religion in the world might go forward and not backward, and not only go forward, but go apace. All the forces of hell were then, and still are, more or less, raised and mustered to oppose the word of the Lord, to hinder its publication and success. We should pray, therefore, that oppositions may be removed, that so the gospel, may have free course to the ears, the hearts, and the consciences of men, that it may be glorified in the conviction and conversion of sinners, the confutation, of gainsayers, and the holy conversation of the saints. God, who magnified the law, and made it honourable, will glorify the gospel, and make that honourable, and so will glorify his own name; and good ministers and good Christians may very well be contented to be little, to be any thing, to be nothing, if Christ be magnified and his gospel be glorified. Paul was now at Athens, or, as some think, at Corinth, and would have the Thessalonians pray that he might have as good success there as he had at Thessalonica, that it might be as well with others even as it was with them. Note, If ministers have been successful in one place, they should desire to be successful in every place where they may preach the gospel. (2.) For the safety of gospel ministers. He asks their prayers, nor for preferment, but for preservation: <hi type="italic">That we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, Those who are enemies to the preaching of the gospel, and persecutors of the faithful preachers of it, are unreasonable and wicked men. They act against all the rules and laws of reason and religion, and are guilty of the greatest absurdity and impiety. Not only in the principles of atheism and infidelity, but also in the practice of the vice and immorality, and especially in persecution, there is the greatest absurdity in the world, as well as impiety. There is need of the spiritual protection, as well as the assistance, of godly and faithful ministers, for these are as the standard-bearers, who are most struck at; and therefore all who wish well to the interest of Christ in the world should pray for them. <hi type="italic">For all men have not faith;</hi> that is, many do not believe the gospel; they will not embrace it themselves, and no wonder if such are restless and malicious in their endeavours to oppose the gospel, decry the ministry, and disgrace the ministers of the word; and too many have not common faith or honesty; there is no confidence that we can safely put in them, and we should pray to be delivered from those who have no conscience nor honour, who never regard what they say or do. We may sometimes be in as much or more danger from false and pretended friends as from open and avowed enemies. <div eID="gen32328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32329" type="x-p"/> II. He encourages them to trust in God. We should not only pray to God for his grace, but also place our trust and confidence in his grace, and humbly expect what we pray for. Observe, <div eID="gen32329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32330" type="x-p"/> 1. What the good is which we may expect from the grace of God-establishment, and preservation from evil; and the best Christians stand in need of these benefits. (1.) That God would establish them. This the apostle had prayed for on their behalf ( <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.17">ch. 2.17</reference>), and now he encourages them to expect this favour. We stand no longer than God holds us up; unless he <hi type="italic">hold up our goings in his paths, our feet will slide,</hi> and we shall fall. (2.) That God will keep them from evil. We have as much need of the grace of God for our perseverance to the end as for the beginning of the good work. The evil of sin is the greatest evil, but there are other evils which God will also preserve his saints from—the evil that is in the world, yea, from all evil, to his heavenly kingdom. <div eID="gen32330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32331" type="x-p"/> 2. What encouragement we have to depend upon the grace of God: <hi type="italic">The Lord is faithful.</hi> He is faithful to his promises, and is the Lord who cannot lie, who will not alter the thing that has gone out of his mouth. When once the promise therefore is made, performance is sure and certain. He is faithful to his relation, a faithful God and a faithful friend; we may depend upon his filling up all the relations he stands in to his people. Let it be our care to be true and faithful in our promises, and to the relations we stand in to this faithful God. He adds, <div eID="gen32331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32332" type="x-p"/> 3. A further ground of hope that God would do this for them, seeing they did and would do the things they were commanded, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.4">v. 4</reference>. The apostle had this confidence in them, and this was founded upon his confidence in God; for there is otherwise no confidence in man. Their obedience is described by doing what he and his fellow-labourers had commanded them, which was no other thing than the commandments of the Lord; for the apostles themselves had no further commission than to teach men <hi type="italic">to observe and to do what the Lord had commanded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 20</reference>. And as the experience the apostle had of their obedience for the time past was one ground of his confidence that they would do the things commanded them for the time to come, so this is one ground to hope that <hi type="italic">whatsoever we ask of God we shall receive of him, because we keep his commandments, and do those things that are pleasing in his sight,</hi> 1 <reference osisRef="John.3.22">John iii. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen32332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32333" type="x-p"/> III. He makes a short prayer for them, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.5">v. 5</reference>. It is a prayer for spiritual blessings. Two things of the greatest importance the apostle prays for:—1. That their hearts may be brought into the love of God, to be in love with God as the most excellent and amiable Being, the best of all beings; and this is not only most reasonable and necessary in order to our happiness, but is our happiness itself; it is a great part of the happiness of heaven itself, where this love shall be made perfect. We can never attain to this unless God by his grace direct our hearts aright, for our love is apt to go astray after other things. Note, We sustain a great deal of damage by misplacing our affections; it is our sin and our misery that we place our affections upon wrong objects. If God directs our love aright upon himself, the rest of the affections will thereby be rectified. 2. That a <hi type="italic">patient waiting for Christ</hi> may be joined with this love of God. There is no true love of God without faith in Jesus Christ. We must wait for Christ, which supposes our faith in him, that we believe he came once in flesh and will come again in glory: and we must expect this second coming of Christ, and be careful to get ready for it; there must be a patient waiting, enduring with courage and constancy all that we may meet with in the mean time: and we <hi type="italic">have need of patience,</hi> and need of divine grace to exercise Christian patience, the <hi type="italic">patience of Christ</hi> (as some read the word), patience for Christ's sake and after Christ's example.
entries.2421a823d525142c280aa6466f59520fa8a67e77: <div eID="gen32333" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions to the Disorderly. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 52.)</title> <div sID="gen32334" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us. <hi type="super">7</hi> For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you; 8 Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you: <hi type="super">9</hi> Not because we have not power, but to make ourselves an ensample unto you to follow us. <hi type="super">10</hi> For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat. <hi type="super">11</hi> For we hear that there are some which walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now them that are such we command and exhort by our Lord Jesus Christ, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread. <hi type="super">13</hi> But ye, brethren, be not weary in well doing. <hi type="super">14</hi> And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed. <hi type="super">15</hi> Yet count <hi type="italic">him</hi> not as an enemy, but admonish <hi type="italic">him</hi> as a brother. <div eID="gen32334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32335" type="x-p"/> The apostle having commended their obedience for the time past, and mentioned his confidence in their obedience for the time to come, proceeds to give them commands and directions to some who were faulty, correcting some things that were amiss among them. Observe, The best society of Christians may have some faulty persons among them, and some things that ought to be reformed. Perfection is not to be found on this side heaven: but evil manners beget good laws; the disorders that Paul heard of as existing among the Thessalonians occasioned the good laws we find in these verses, which are of constant use to us, and all others whom they may concern. Observe, <div eID="gen32335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32336" type="x-p"/> I. That which was amiss among the Thessalonians, which is expressed, <div eID="gen32336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32337" type="x-p"/> 1. More generally. There were some who <hi type="italic">walked disorderly, not after the tradition they received</hi> from the apostle, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.6">v. 6</reference>. Some of the brethren were guilty of this disorderly walking; they did not live regularly, nor govern themselves according to the rules of Christianity, nor agreeably to their profession of religion; not according to the precepts delivered by the apostle, which they had received, and pretended to pay a regard to. Note, It is required of those who have received the gospel, and who profess a subjection to it, that they live according to the gospel. If they do not, they are to be counted disorderly persons. <div eID="gen32337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32338" type="x-p"/> 2. In particular, there were among them some <hi type="italic">idle persons and busy-bodies,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.11">v. 11</reference>. This the apostle was so credibly informed of that he had sufficient reason to give commands and directions with relation to such persons, how they ought to behave, and how the church should act towards them. (1.) There were some among them who were idle, <hi type="italic">not working at all,</hi> or doing nothing. It does not appear that they were gluttons or drunkards, but idle, and therefore disorderly people. It is not enough for any to say they do no hurt; for it is required of all persons that they do good in the places and relations in which Providence has placed them. It is probable that these persons had a notion (by misunderstanding some passages in the former epistle) concerning the near approach of the coming of Christ, which served them for a pretence to leave off the work of their callings, and live in idleness. Note, It is a great error, or abuse of religion, to make it a cloak for idleness or any other sin. If we were sure that the day of judgment were ever so near, we must, notwithstanding, do the work of the day in its day, that when our Lord comes he may find us doing. The servant who waits for the coming of his Lord aright must be working as his Lord has commanded, that all may be ready when he comes. Or, it may be, these disorderly persons pretended that the liberty wherewith Christ had made them free discharged them from the services and business of their particular callings and employments in the world: where as they were <hi type="italic">to abide in the same calling wherein they were called of God, and therein abide with God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20">1 Cor. vii. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.24">24</reference>. Industry in our particular callings as men is a duty required of us by our general calling as Christians. Or perhaps the general charity there was then among Christians to their poor brethren encouraged some to live in idleness, as knowing the church would maintain them: whatever was the cause, they were much to blame. (2.) There were busy-bodies among them: and it should seem, by the connection, that the same persons who were idle were busy-bodies also. This may seem to be a contradiction; but so it is, that most commonly those persons who have no business of their own to do, or who neglect it, busy themselves in other men's matters. If we are idle, the devil and a corrupt heart will soon find us something to do. The mind of man is a busy thing; if it be not employed in doing good, it will be doing evil. Note, Busy-bodies are disorderly walkers, such as are guilty of vain curiosity, and impertinent meddling with things that do not concern them, and troubling themselves and others with other men's matters. The apostle warns Timothy (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.13">1 Tim. v. 13</reference>) to beware of such <hi type="italic">as learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house, and are not only idle, but tatlers also, and busy-bodies, speaking things which they ought not.</hi> <div eID="gen32338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32339" type="x-p"/> II. The good laws which were occasioned by these evil manners, concerning which we may take notice, <div eID="gen32339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32340" type="x-p"/> 1. Whose laws they are: they are commands of the apostles of our Lord, given in the name of their Lord and ours, that is, the commands of our Lord himself. <hi type="italic">We command you, brethren, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.6">v. 6</reference>. Again, <hi type="italic">We command and exhort you by our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.12">v. 12</reference>. The apostle uses words of authority and entreaty: and, where disorders are to be rectified or prevented, there is need of both. The authority of Christ should awe our minds to obedience, and his grace and goodness should allure us. <div eID="gen32340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32341" type="x-p"/> 2. What the good laws and rules are. The apostle gives directions to the whole church, commands to those disorderly persons, and an exhortation to those in particular who did well among them. <div eID="gen32341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32342" type="x-p"/> (1.) His commands and directions to the whole church regard, [1.] Their behaviour towards the disorderly persons who were among them, which is thus expressed (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.6">v. 6</reference>), to <hi type="italic">withdraw themselves from such,</hi> and afterwards to <hi type="italic">mark that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed; yet not to count him as an enemy, but to admonish him as a brother.</hi> The directions of the apostle are carefully to be observed in our conduct towards disorderly persons. We must be very cautious in church-censures and church-discipline. We must, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Note that man who is suspected or charged with not obeying the word of God, or walking contrary thereto, that is, we must have sufficient proof of his fault before we proceed further. We must, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Admonish him in a friendly manner; we must put him in mind of his sin, and of his duty; and this should be done privately (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.15">Matt. xviii. 15</reference>); then, if he will not hear, we must, <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Withdraw from him, and not keep company with him, that is, we must avoid familiar converse and society with such, for two reasons, namely, that we may not learn his evil ways; for he who follows vain and idle persons, and keeps company with such, is in danger of becoming like them. Another reason is for the shaming, and so the reforming, of those that offend, that when idle and disorderly persons see how their loose practices are disliked by all wise and good people they may be ashamed of them, and walk more orderly. Love therefore to the persons of our offending brethren, even when we hate their vices, should be the motive of our withdrawing from them; and even those who are under the censures of the church must not be accounted as enemies (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.15">v. 15</reference>); for, if they be reclaimed and reformed by these censures, they will recover their credit and comfort, and right to church-privileges as brethren. [2.] Their general conduct and behaviour ought to be according to the good example the apostle and those who were with him had given them: <hi type="italic">Yourselves know how you ought to follow us,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.7">v. 7</reference>. Those who planted religion among them had set a good example before them; and the ministers of the gospel should be ensamples to the flock. It is the duty of Christians not only to walk according to the traditions of the apostles, and the doctrines they preached, but also according to the good example they set before them, <hi type="italic">to be followers of them so far as they were followers of Christ.</hi> The particular good example the apostle mentions was their diligence, which was so different from what was found in the disorderly walkers he takes notice of: "<hi type="italic">We behaved not ourselves disorderly among you</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.7">v. 7</reference>), we did not spend our time idly, in idle visits, idle talk, idle sports." They took pains in their ministry, in preaching the gospel, and in getting their own living. <hi type="italic">Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">v. 8</reference>. Though he might justly have demanded a maintenance, because those who preach the gospel may of right expect to live by the gospel. This is a just debt that people owe to their ministers, and the apostle had power or authority to have demanded this (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.9">v. 9</reference>); but he waived his right from affection to them, and for the sake of the gospel, and that he might be an example for them to follow (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.9">v. 9</reference>), that they might learn how to fill up time, and always be employed in something that would turn to good account. <div eID="gen32342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32343" type="x-p"/> (2.) He commands and directs those that live idle lives to reform, and set themselves to their business. He had given commandments to this purport, as well as a good example of this, when he was among them: <hi type="italic">Even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any man would not work neither should he eat,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.10">v. 10</reference>. It was a proverbial speech among the Jews, <hi type="italic">He who does not labour does not deserve to eat.</hi> The labourer is worthy of his meat; but what is the loiterer worthy of? It is the will of God that every man should have a calling, and mind his calling, and make a business of it, and that none should live like useless drones in the world. Such persons do what in them lies to defeat the sentence, <hi type="italic">In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat thy bread.</hi> It was not the mere humour of the apostle, who was an active stirring man himself and therefore would have every body else to be so too, but it was the command of our Lord Jesus Christ, that <hi type="italic">with quietness we work, and eat our own bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.12">v. 12</reference>. Men ought some way or other to earn their own living, otherwise they do not eat their own bread. Observe, There must be work or labour, in opposition to idleness; and there must be quietness, in opposition to being busy-bodies in other men's matters. We must study to be quiet, and do our own business. This is an excellent but rare composition, to be of an active yet quiet spirit, active in our own business and yet quiet as to other people's. <div eID="gen32343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32344" type="x-p"/> (3.) He exhorts <hi type="italic">those that did well not to</hi> be <hi type="italic">weary in well-doing</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.13">v. 13</reference>); as if he had said, "Go on and prosper. The Lord is with you while you are with him. See that whatever you do, that is good, you persevere therein. Hold on your way, and hold out to the end. You must never give over, nor tire in your work. It will be time enough to rest when you come to heaven, that <hi type="italic">everlasting rest which remains for the people of God.</hi>"
entries.73f2227898c4d2a612f85bc2b2c040835f8f3ea0: <div eID="gen32344" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Apostolic Benediction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 52.)</title> <div sID="gen32345" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Now the Lord of peace himself give you peace always by all means. The Lord <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you all. <hi type="super">17</hi> The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write. <hi type="super">18</hi> The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you all. Amen. <div eID="gen32345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32346" type="x-p"/> In this conclusion of the epistle we have the apostle's benediction and prayers for these Thessalonians. Let us desire them for ourselves and our friend. There are three blessings pronounced upon them, or desired for them:— <div eID="gen32346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32347" type="x-p"/> I. That God would give them peace. Note, 1. Peace is the blessing pronounced or desired. By peace we may understand all manner of prosperity; here it may signify, in particular, peace with God, peace in their own minds and consciences, peace among themselves, and peace with all men. 2. This peace is desired for them always, or in every thing; and he desired they might have all good things at all times. 3. Peace by all means: that, as they enjoyed the means of grace, they might with success use all the means and methods of peace too; for peace is often difficult, as it is always desirable. 4. That God would give them peace, who is the Lord of peace. If we have any peace that is desirable, God must give it, who is the <hi type="italic">author of peace and lover of concord.</hi> We shall neither have peaceable dispositions ourselves nor find men disposed to be at peace with us, unless the God of peace give us both. <div eID="gen32347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32348" type="x-p"/> II. That the presence of God might be with them: <hi type="italic">The Lord be with you all.</hi> We need nothing more to make us safe and happy, nor can we desire any thing better for ourselves and our friends, than to have God's gracious presence with us and them. This will be a guide and guard in every way that we may go, and our comfort in every condition we may be in. It is the presence of God that makes heaven to be heaven, and this will make this earth to be like heaven. No matter where we are if God be with us, nor who is absent if God be with us, nor who is absent if God be present with us. <div eID="gen32348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32349" type="x-p"/> III. That the <hi type="italic">grace of our Lord Jesus Christ might be with them.</hi> So this apostle concluded his first epistle to these Thessalonians; and it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ that we may comfortably hope to have peace with God and enjoy the presence of God, for he has made those nigh that were afar off. It is this grace that is all in all to make us happy. This is what the apostle admired and magnified on all occasions, what he delighted and trusted in; and by this salutation or benediction, written with his own hand, as the token of every epistle (when the rest was written by an amanuensis), he took care lest the churches he wrote to should be imposed on by counterfeit epistles, which he knew would be of dangerous consequence. <div eID="gen32349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32350" type="x-p"/> Let us be thankful that we have the canon of scripture complete, and by the wonderful and special care of divine Providence preserved pure and uncorrupt through so many successive ages, and not dare to add to it, nor diminish from it. Let us believe the divine original of the sacred scriptures, and conform our faith and practice to this our sufficient and only rule, <hi type="italic">which is able to make us wise unto salvation, through faith which is in Christ Jesus.</hi> Amen.  <chapter eID="2Thess.3"/> <div eID="gen32350" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen32265" osisID="2Thess" type="book"/>

entries.8d7229f06a7d92e8e66780f9c62043d23d5f7ea1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18038"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen36988" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.1-2Thess.3.18">2Th 3:1-18</reference>. He Asks Their Prayers: His Confidence in Them: Prayer for Them: Charges against Disorderly Idle Conduct; His Own Example: Concluding Prayer and Salutation.<div eID="gen36988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36989" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18038"/><hi type="bold">1. Finally--</hi>literally, "As to what remains."<div eID="gen36989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">may have free course--</hi>literally, "may run"; spread rapidly without a drag on the wheels of its course. That the new-creating word may "run," as "swiftly" as the creative word at the first (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.15">Psa 147:15</reference>). The opposite is the word of God being "bound" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.9">2Ti 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen36990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glorified--</hi>by sinners accepting it (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.48">Ac 13:48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.23">Ga 1:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">24</reference>). Contrast "evil spoken of" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>).<div eID="gen36991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it is with you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.6">1Th 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10">4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.11">5:11</reference>). <div eID="gen36992" type="x-p"/>
entries.e35ae671525928faf15d8100fbf5468ac10c896f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18039"/><div sID="gen36993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18039"/><hi type="bold">2. that we ... be delivered from unreasonable ... men--</hi>literally, men out of place, inept, unseemly: out of the way bad: more than ordinarily bad. An undesigned coincidence with <reference osisRef="Acts.18.5-Acts.18.9">Ac 18:5-9</reference>. Paul was now at Corinth, where the Jews "opposed themselves" to his preaching: in answer to his prayers and those of his converts at Thessalonica and elsewhere, "the Lord, in vision," assured him of exemption from "the hurt," and of success in bringing in "much people." On the unreasonable, out-of-the way perversity of the Jews, as known to the Thessalonians, see <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1Th 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">16</reference>.<div eID="gen36993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36994" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have not faith--</hi>or as Greek, "the faith" of the Christian: the only antidote to what is "unreasonable and wicked." The Thessalonians, from their ready acceptance of the Gospel (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">6</reference>), might think "all" would similarly receive it; but the Jews were far from having such a readiness to believe the truth. <div eID="gen36994" type="x-p"/>
entries.2300666a032a3e125ee3278d8fcfd7f87ca75dba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18040"/><div sID="gen36995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18040"/><hi type="bold">3. faithful--</hi>alluding to "faith" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.2">2Th 3:2</reference>): though many will not believe, the Lord (other very old manuscripts read "God") is still to be believed in as faithful to His promises (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.24">1Th 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.13">2Ti 2:13</reference>). Faith on the part of man answers to faithfulness on the part of God.<div eID="gen36995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stablish you--</hi>as he had prayed (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.17">2Th 2:17</reference>). Though it was on himself that wicked men were making their onset, he turns away from asking the Thessalonians' prayers for HIS deliverance (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.2">2Th 3:2</reference>: so unselfish was he, even in religion), to express his assurance of THEIR establishment in the faith, and preservation from evil. This assurance thus exactly answers to his prayer for them (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.17">2Th 2:17</reference>), "Our Lord ... stablish you in every good word and work." He has before his mind the Lord's Prayer, "Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil"; where, as here, the translation may be, "from the evil one"; the great hinderer of "every good word and work." Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.13.19">Mt 13:19</reference>, "the wicked one." <div eID="gen36996" type="x-p"/>
entries.43a14b4ee75bad1e856d8ab16ce7fa59ddae6b32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18041"/><div sID="gen36997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18041"/><hi type="bold">4. we have confidence in the Lord--</hi>as "faithful" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.3">2Th 3:3</reference>). Have confidence in no man when left to himself [Bengel].<div eID="gen36997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ye both do--</hi>Some of the oldest manuscripts insert a clause, "that ye both have done" before, "and are doing, and will do." He means the majority by "ye," not all of them (compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.11">2Th 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.3">2Th 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.6">1Th 3:6</reference>). <div eID="gen36998" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca12d18844977e88341ac1f9f83cb5fbb7c8bccc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18042"/><div sID="gen36999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18042"/>5. If "the Lord" be here the Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">2Co 3:17</reference>), the three Persons of the Trinity will occur in this verse.<div eID="gen36999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love of God--</hi>love to God.<div eID="gen37000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">patient waiting for Christ--</hi>rather as Greek, "the patience (endurance) of Christ," namely, which Christ showed [Alford] (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.3">1Th 1:3</reference>). Estius, however, supports English Version (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.9">Re 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>). At all events, this grace, "patience," or persevering endurance, is connected with the "hope" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.3">1Th 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>) of Christ's coming. In Alford's translation we may compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference>, "Run with patience (endurance) ... looking to Jesus ... who, for the joy that was before Him, endured the cross"; so WE are to endure, as looking for the hope to be realized at His coming (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.36">He 10:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.37">37</reference>). <div eID="gen37001" type="x-p"/>
entries.54c21161a4bf3fc2bd44d9c9e3011be7ebdeb9a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18043"/><div sID="gen37002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18043"/><hi type="bold">6. we command you--</hi>Hereby he puts to a particular test their obedience in general to his commands, which obedience he had recognized in <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.4">2Th 3:4</reference>.<div eID="gen37002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">withdraw--</hi>literally, "to furl the sails"; as we say, to steer clear of (compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.14">2Th 3:14</reference>). Some had given up labor as though the Lord's day was immediately coming. He had enjoined mild censure of such in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.14">1Th 5:14</reference>, "Warn ... the unruly"; but now that the mischief had become more confirmed, he enjoins stricter discipline, namely, withdrawal from their company (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.11">1Co 5:11</reference>; 2Jo 10, 11): not a formal sentence of excommunication, such as was subsequently passed on more heinous offenders (as in <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">1Co 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>). He says "brother," that is, professing Christian; for in the case of unprofessing heathen, believers needed not be so strict (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.10-1Cor.5.13">1Co 5:10-13</reference>).<div eID="gen37003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">disorderly--</hi>Paul plainly would not have sanctioned the order of Mendicant Friars, who reduce such a "disorderly" and lazy life to a system. Call it not an order, but a burden to the community (Bengel, alluding to the Greek, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">2Th 3:8</reference>, for "be chargeable," literally, "be a burden").<div eID="gen37004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the tradition--</hi>the oral instruction which he had given to them when present (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.10">2Th 3:10</reference>), and subsequently committed to writing (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.11">1Th 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen37005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which he received of us--</hi>Some oldest manuscripts read, "ye received"; others, "they received." The English Version reading has no very old authority. <div eID="gen37006" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4c264f79c9ebcf906d34939047147e17bfee993: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18044"/><div sID="gen37007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18044"/><hi type="bold">7. how ye ought to follow us--</hi>how ye ought to live so as to "imitate (so the Greek for 'follow') us" (compare Notes, see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1Co 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.6">1Th 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen37007" type="x-p"/>
entries.16958155502d7da976d17baf0a9365d374ba5507: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18045"/><div sID="gen37008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18045"/><hi type="bold">8. eat any man's bread--</hi>Greek, "eat bread from any man," that is, live at anyone's expense. Contrast <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.12">2Th 3:12</reference>, "eat THEIR OWN bread."<div eID="gen37008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrought--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.20.34">Ac 20:34</reference>). In both Epistles they state they maintained themselves by labor; but in this second Epistle they do so in order to offer themselves herein as an example to the idle; whereas, in the first, their object in doing so is to vindicate themselves from all imputation of mercenary motives in preaching the Gospel (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.5">1Th 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>) [Edmunds]. They preached gratuitously though they might have claimed maintenance from their converts.<div eID="gen37009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labour and travail--</hi>"toil and hardship" (see on <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night and day--</hi>scarcely allowing time for repose.<div eID="gen37011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chargeable--</hi>Greek, "a burden," or "burdensome." The Philippians did not regard it as a burden to contribute to his support (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">Php 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">16</reference>), sending to him while he was in this very Thessalonica (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.15">Ac 16:15</reference>, 34, 40). Many Thessalonians, doubtless, would have felt it a privilege to contribute, but as he saw some idlers among them who would have made a pretext of his example to justify themselves, he waived his right. His reason for the same course at Corinth was to mark how different were his aims from those of the false teachers who sought their own lucre (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.13">12, 13</reference>). It is at the very time and place of writing these Epistles that Paul is expressly said to have wrought at tent-making with Aquila (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">Ac 18:3</reference>); an undesigned coincidence. <div eID="gen37012" type="x-p"/>
entries.20d0807dba993552eda9bff4213f4ed294527e02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18046"/><div sID="gen37013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18046"/>9. (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.4-1Cor.9.6">1Co 9:4-6</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.6">Ga 6:6</reference>.) <div eID="gen37013" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1ca0244f67082688f92fa71f42a7ab10e393df5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18047"/><div sID="gen37014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18047"/><hi type="bold">10. For even--</hi>Translate, "For also." We not only set you the example, but gave a positive "command."<div eID="gen37014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commanded--</hi>Greek imperfect, "We were commanding"; we kept charge of you.<div eID="gen37015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">would not work--</hi>Greek, "is unwilling to work." Bengel makes this to be the argument: not that such a one is to have his food withdrawn from him by others; but he proves from the necessity of eating the necessity of working; using this pleasantry, Let him who will not work show himself an angel, that is, do without food as the angels do (but since he cannot do without food, then he ought to be not unwilling to work). It seems to me simpler to take it as a punishment of the idle. Paul often quotes good adages current among the people, stamping them with inspired approval. In the Hebrew, "Bereshith Rabba," the same saying is found; and in the book Zeror, "He who will not work before the sabbath, must not eat on the sabbath." <div eID="gen37016" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4c91474f2fac591b6791fbffe496b56bc536787: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18048"/><div sID="gen37017" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18048"/><hi type="bold">11. busy bodies--</hi>In the Greek the similarity of sound marks the antithesis, "Doing none of their own business, yet overdoing in the business of others." Busy about everyone's business but their own. "Nature abhors a vacuum"; so if not doing one's own business, one is apt to meddle with his neighbor's business. Idleness is the parent of busybodies (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.13">1Ti 5:13</reference>). Contrast <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.11">1Th 4:11</reference>. <div eID="gen37017" type="x-p"/>
entries.398fdecd217856c85262b5afcb6f176a4ee98fe8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18049"/><div sID="gen37018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18049"/><hi type="bold">12. by--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "IN the Lord Jesus." So the Greek, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.1">1Th 4:1</reference>, implying the sphere wherein such conduct is appropriate and consistent. "We exhort you thus, as ministers IN Christ, exhorting our people IN Christ."<div eID="gen37018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with quietness--</hi>quiet industry; laying aside restless, bustling, intermeddling officiousness (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.11">2Th 3:11</reference>).<div eID="gen37019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their own--</hi>bread earned by themselves, not another's bread (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">2Th 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen37020" type="x-p"/>
entries.f845886efdd3806d8260050ae6aad9a21d18c699: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18050"/><div sID="gen37021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18050"/><hi type="bold">13. be not weary--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "Be not cowardly in"; do not be wanting in strenuousness in doing well. Edmunds explains it: Do not culpably neglect to do well, namely, with patient industry do your duty in your several callings. In contrast to the "disorderly, not-working busybodies" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.11">2Th 3:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.6.9">Ga 6:9</reference>). <div eID="gen37021" type="x-p"/>
entries.39cf2feb2a5a9fd772445e6291a4a4594421a408: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18051"/><div sID="gen37022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18051"/><hi type="bold">14. note that man--</hi>mark him in your own mind as one to be avoided (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.6">2Th 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen37022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he may be ashamed--</hi>Greek, "made to turn and look into himself, and so be put to shame." Feeling himself shunned by godly brethren, he may become ashamed of his course. <div eID="gen37023" type="x-p"/>
entries.f421a893f2ffb4b462ef9171921fa151e69870e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18052"/><div sID="gen37024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18052"/><hi type="bold">15. admonish him as a brother--</hi>not yet excommunicated (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Le 19:17</reference>). Do not shun him in contemptuous silence, but tell him why he is so avoided (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.15">Mt 18:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.14">1Th 5:14</reference>). <div eID="gen37024" type="x-p"/>
entries.904dc84f6b2858c3ff57562361ea6d5e5f0253d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18053"/><div sID="gen37025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18053"/><hi type="bold">16. Lord of peace--</hi>Jesus Christ. The same title is given to Him as to the Father, "the God of peace" (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.33">Ro 15:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.20">16:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.11">2Co 13:11</reference>). An appropriate title in the prayer here, where the harmony of the Christian community was liable to interruption from the "disorderly." The Greek article requires the translation, "Give you the peace" which it is "His to give." "Peace" outward and inward, here and hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Ro 14:17</reference>).<div eID="gen37025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">always--</hi>unbroken, not changing with outward circumstances.<div eID="gen37026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by all means--</hi>Greek, "in every way." Most of the oldest manuscripts read, "in every place"; thus he prays for their peace in all times ("always") and places.<div eID="gen37027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord be with you all--</hi>May He bless you not only with peace, but also with His presence (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>). Even the disorderly brethren (compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.15">2Th 3:15</reference>, "a brother") are included in this prayer. <div eID="gen37028" type="x-p"/>
entries.76be434bd7283cdbeb5f5d2c5aaab58aabff8094: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18054"/><div sID="gen37029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18054"/>17. The Epistle was written by an amanuensis (perhaps Silas or Timothy), and only the closing salutation written by Paul's "own hand" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.16.22">Ro 16:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.21">1Co 16:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.18">Col 4:18</reference>). Wherever Paul does not subjoin this autograph salutation, we may presume he wrote the whole Epistle himself (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.11">Ga 6:11</reference>).<div eID="gen37029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>which autograph salutation.<div eID="gen37030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the token--</hi>to distinguish genuine Epistles from spurious ones put forth in my name (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen37031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in every epistle--</hi>Some think he signed his name to every Epistle with his own hand; but as there is no trace of this in any manuscripts of all the Epistles, it is more likely that he alludes to his writing with his own hand in closing every Epistle, even in those Epistles (Romans, Second Corinthians, Ephesians, Philippians, First Thessalonians) wherein he does not specify his having done so.<div eID="gen37032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so I write--</hi>so I sign my name: this is a specimen of my handwriting, by which to distinguish my geniune letters from forgeries. <div eID="gen37033" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4c6c218e8162990856c6985c116e2225e80a273: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18055"/><div sID="gen37034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18055"/>18. He closes every Epistle by praying for GRACE to those whom he addresses.<div eID="gen37034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Amen--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts It was doubtless the response of the congregation after hearing the Epistle read publicly; hence it crept into copies.<div eID="gen37035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37036" type="x-p"/> The Subscription is spurious, as the Epistle was written not "from Athens," but from Corinth.  <chapter eID="2Thess.3"/><div eID="gen37036" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen36868" osisID="2Thess" type="book"/>

entries.79173775323071e8e9d5edd1f047cbd5ad53fc03: <div eID="gen51383" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51384" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51385" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51385" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51384" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51386" type="x-p"/> The apostle recommends himself and his brethren to the prayers of the Church, that their preaching might be successful, and that they might be delivered from wicked men, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.1">2Thes 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.2">2Thes 3:2</reference>. Expresses his confidence in God and them, and prays that they may patiently wait for the coming of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.3-2Thes.3.5">2Thes 3:3-5</reference>. Gives them directions concerning strict discipline in the Church; and shows how he and his fellow laborers had behaved among them, not availing themselves of their own power and authority, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.6-2Thes.3.9">2Thes 3:6-9</reference>. Shows them how to treat disorderly and idle people, and not to get weary in well doing, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.10-2Thes.3.13">2Thes 3:10-13</reference>. Directs them not to associate with those who obey not the orders contained in this epistle, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.14">2Thes 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.15">2Thes 3:15</reference>, Prays that they may have increasing peace, 16, And concludes with his salutation and benediction, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.17">2Thes 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.18">2Thes 3:18</reference>. <div eID="gen51386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51387" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51388" type="x-p"/> Finally, brethren - The words το λοιπον do not mean finally, but, furthermore - to come to a conclusion - what remains is this - I shall only add - any of these phrases expresses the sense of the original. <div eID="gen51388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51389" type="x-p"/> Pray for us - God, in the order of his grace and providence, has made even the success of his Gospel dependent, in a certain measure, on the prayers of his followers. Why he should do so we cannot tell, but that he has done so we know; and they are not a little criminal who neglect to make fervent supplications for the prosperity of the cause of God. <div eID="gen51389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51390" type="x-p"/> May have free course - They were to pray that the doctrine of the Lord, ὁ λογος του Κυριου, might run, τρεχῃ, an allusion to the races in the Olympic games: that, as it had already got into the stadium or race course, and had started fairly, so it might run on, get to the goal, and be glorified; i.e., gain the crown, appointed for him that should get first to the end of the course.
entries.a783bc4441410c7cef1ae6908361f22acc0754c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51391" type="x-p"/> Unreasonable and wicked men - The word ατοπων, which we translate unreasonable, signifies rather disorderly, unmanageable; persons out of their place - under no discipline, regardless of law and restraint, and ever acting agreeably to the disorderly and unreasonable impulse of their own minds. <div eID="gen51391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51392" type="x-p"/> For all men have not faith - The word πιστις is without doubt, to be taken here for fidelity or trustworthiness, and not for faith; and this is agreeable to the meaning given to it in the very next verse: But the Lord is faithful, πιστος δε εστιν ὁ Κυριος. <div eID="gen51392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51393" type="x-p"/> There are many, even of those who have received a measure of the Divine light, in whom we cannot confide; they are irregular, disorderly, and cannot be brought under regular discipline: to these we cannot trust either ourselves or any thing that concerns the cause of God. But the Lord is worthy of your whole confidence; doubt him not; he will establish you, and keep you from any evil to which you may be exposed by these or such like persons.
entries.68a524d3574b451c1495204c57b41f1652c190c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51394" type="x-p"/> From evil - Απο του πονηρου may be translated, from the devil or from the evil one. They had disorderly men, wicked men, and the evil one or the devil, to contend with; God alone could support and give them the victory; he had promised to do it, and he might ever be confided in as being invariably faithful.
entries.e38b3fe29bf1ee41cf9f9edb7cc111dfbef1e40a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen51394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51395" type="x-p"/> And we have confidence - We have no doubt of God's kindness towards you; he loves you, and will support you: and we can confide in you, that ye are now acting as we have desired you, and will continue so to do.
entries.5215c31d2feaf77720cae3813dc560f57d60a506: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen51395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51396" type="x-p"/> The Lord direct your hearts into the love of God - The love of God is the grand motive and principle of obedience; this must occupy your hearts: the heart is irregular in all its workings; God alone, by his Spirit, can direct it into his love, and keep it right; κατευθυναι, give a proper direction to all its passions, and keep them in order, regularity and purity. <div eID="gen51396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51397" type="x-p"/> The patience of Christ - Such patience, under all your sufferings and persecutions, as Christ manifested under his. He bore meekly the contradiction of sinners against himself; and when he was reviled, he reviled not again.
entries.0622c096de47a4129d72ddbe9c1d4dbde3395533: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen51397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51398" type="x-p"/> That ye withdraw yourselves - Have no fellowship with those who will not submit to proper discipline; who do not keep their place; ατακτως, such as are out of their rank, and act according to their own wills and caprices; and particularly such as are idle and busybodies. These he had ordered, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.11">1Thes 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.12">1Thes 4:12</reference>, that they should study to be quiet, mind their own business, and work with their hands; but it appears that they had paid no attention to this order, and now he desires the Church to exclude such from their communion. <div eID="gen51398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51399" type="x-p"/> And not after the tradition - This evidently refers to the orders contained in the first epistle; and that first epistle was the tradition which they had received from him. It was, therefore, no unwritten word, no uncertain saying, handed about from one to another; but a part of the revelation which God had given, and which they found in the body of his epistle. These are the only traditions which the Church of God is called to regard.
entries.2e58abfc14f3d508f2fc5b0365cfacdde43a2c8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen51399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51400" type="x-p"/> We behaved not ourselves disorderly - Ουκ ητακτησαμεν· We did not go out of our rank - we kept our place, and discharged all its duties.
entries.9043f2a5d485615dc3a17d7aa1973e13d7061761: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen51400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51401" type="x-p"/> Neither did we eat any man's bread for naught - We paid for what we bought, and worked with our hands that we might have money to buy what was necessary. <div eID="gen51401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51402" type="x-p"/> Labour and travail night and day - We were incessantly employed, either in preaching the Gospel, visiting from house to house, or working at our calling. As it is very evident that the Church at Thessalonica was very pious, and most affectionately attached to the apostle, they must have been very poor, seeing he was obliged to work hard to gain himself the necessaries of life. Had they been able to support him he would not have worked with labor and travail night and day, that he might not be burdensome to them; and, as we may presume that they were very poor, he could not have got his support among them without adding to their burdens. To this his generous mind could not submit; it is no wonder, therefore, that he is so severe against those who would not labor, but were a burden to the poor followers of God.
entries.82eae644687e937cb1914e90934e05a9cf8ef862: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen51402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51403" type="x-p"/> Not because we have not power - We have the power, εξουσιαν, the right, to be maintained by those in whose behalf we labor. The laborer is worthy of his hire, is a maxim universally acknowledged and respected; and they who preach the Gospel should live by the Gospel: the apostle did not claim his privilege, but labored for his own support, that he might be an example to those whom he found otherwise disposed, and that he might spare the poor. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.1">1Cor 9:1</reference>, etc.
entries.488930b4fe165616a24c475dd2b2e9571fbc95b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen51403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51404" type="x-p"/> If any would not work, neither should he eat - This is a just maxim, and universal nature inculcates it to man. If man will work, he may eat; if he do not work, he neither can eat, nor should he eat. The maxim is founded on these words of the Lord: In the sweat of thy brow thou shall eat bread. Industry is crowned with God's blessing; idleness is loaded with his curse. This maxim was a proverb among the Jews. Men who can work, and will rather support themselves by begging, should not get one morsel of bread. It is a sin to minister to necessities that are merely artificial.
entries.36f775a46d45f1a88d079475d86005dcf5d5ad63: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen51404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51405" type="x-p"/> For we hear that there are some - It is very likely that St. Paul kept up some sort of correspondence with the Thessalonian Church; for he had heard every thing that concerned their state, and it was from this information that he wrote his second epistle. <div eID="gen51405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51406" type="x-p"/> Disorderly - Ατακτως· Out of their rank - not keeping their own place. <div eID="gen51406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51407" type="x-p"/> Working not at all - Either lounging at home, or becoming religious gossips; μηδεν εργαζομενους, doing nothing. <div eID="gen51407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51408" type="x-p"/> Busybodies - Περιεργαζομενους· Doing every thing they should not do - impertinent meddlers with other people's business; prying into other people's circumstances and domestic affairs; magnifying or minifying, mistaking or underrating, every thing; newsmongers and telltales; an abominable race, the curse of every neighborhood where they live, and a pest to religious society. There is a fine paronomasia in the above words, and evidently intended by the apostle.
entries.d2840b17415c9faf9d3ed9bbef0e31b647fb2078: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen51408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51409" type="x-p"/> With quietness they work - Μετα ἡσυχιας· With silence; leaving their tale-bearing and officious intermeddling. Less noise and more work! <div eID="gen51409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51410" type="x-p"/> That - they work, and eat their own bread - Their own bread, because earned by their own honest industry. What a degrading thing to live on the bounty or mercy of another, while a man is able to acquire his own livelihood! He who can submit to this has lost the spirit of independence; and has in him a beggar's heart, and is capable of nothing but base and beggarly actions. Witness the great mass of the people of England, who by their dependence on the poor rates are, from being laborious, independent, and respect able, become idle, profligate, and knavish; the propagators and perpetrators of crime; a discredit to the nation, and a curse to society. The apostle's command is a cure for such; and the Church of God should discountenance such, and disown them.
entries.483979bcbc794b885c1557b114e9a6f5c8f3d50a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen51410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51411" type="x-p"/> Be not weary in well-doing - While ye stretch out no hand of relief to the indolent and lazy, do not forget the real poor - the genuine representatives of an impoverished Christ; and rather relieve a hundred undeserving objects, than pass by one who is a real object of charity.
entries.08b571d745bb66f470ab32c5c3878e4a115d8d19: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen51411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51412" type="x-p"/> If any man obey not - They had disobeyed his word in the first epistle, and the Church still continued to bear with them; now he tells the Church, if they still continue to disregard what is said to them, and particularly his word by this second epistle, they are to mark them as being totally incorrigible, and have no fellowship with them. <div eID="gen51412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51413" type="x-p"/> Some construe the words δια της επιστολης with τουτον σημειουσθε· Give me information of that man by a letter - let me hear of his continued obstinacy, and send me his name. This was probably in order to excommunicate him, and deliver him over to Satan for the destruction of the body, that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. The words of the original will bear either construction, that in the text, or that given above.
entries.93555387dd6208d1dd5fda27b18d57c4c235c108: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen51413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51414" type="x-p"/> Count him not as an enemy - Consider him still more an enemy to himself than to you; and admonish him as a brother, though you have ceased to hold religious communion with him. His soul is still of infinite value; labor to get it saved.
entries.0cf20a24072ed0daa84678ce3cfde55a1ab1fc09: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen51414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51415" type="x-p"/> The Lord of peace - Jesus Christ, who is called our peace, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Eph 2:14</reference>; and The Prince of peace, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference>. May he give you peace, for he is the Fountain and Dispenser of it. <div eID="gen51415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51416" type="x-p"/> Always - Both in your own consciences, and among yourselves. <div eID="gen51416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51417" type="x-p"/> By all means - Παντι τροπῳ· By all means, methods, occasions, instruments, and occurrences; peace or prosperity in every form and shape. <div eID="gen51417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51418" type="x-p"/> Instead of εν παντι τροπῳ, in every way, etc., εν παντι τοπῳ, in every place, is the reading of A*D*FG, some others; with the Vulgate and Itala. Chrysostom, Ambrosiaster, Augustine, and others, have the same reading: May God grant you prosperity always, and everywhere. <div eID="gen51418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51419" type="x-p"/> The Lord be with you all - This is agreeable to the promise of our Lord: Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world; <reference osisRef="Mat.28.20">Mat 28:20</reference>. May the Lord, who has promised to be always with his true disciples, be with you! Christians are the temple of God, and the temple of God has the Divine presence in it. May you ever continue to be his Church, that the Lord God may dwell among you!
entries.75362f392f3509e1810e54b1ce6ce336b673d46a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen51419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51420" type="x-p"/> The salutation of Paul with mine own hand - It is very likely that Paul employed an amanuensis generally, either to write what he dictated, or to make a fair copy of what he wrote. In either case the apostle always subscribed it, and wrote the salutation and benediction with his own hand; and this was what authenticated all his epistles. A measure of this kind would be very necessary if forged epistles were carried about in those times. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.21">1Cor 16:21</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Col.4.18">Col 4:18</reference> (note).
entries.555b4c8829199970a3dbf16eef56b948277033a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen51420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51421" type="x-p"/> The grace - The favor, blessing, and influence of our Lord Jesus Christ, be with you all - be your constant companion. May you ever feel his presence, and enjoy his benediction! <div eID="gen51421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51422" type="x-p"/> Amen - So let be! God grant it! This word in this place, has more evidence in favor of its genuineness than it has in most other places; and was probably added here by the apostle himself, or by the Church of the Thessalonians. <div eID="gen51422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51423" type="x-p"/> The subscriptions to this epistle are various in the MSS. and Versions. The latter are as follows: - <div eID="gen51423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51424" type="x-p"/> The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians was written from Athens. - Common Greek text. <div eID="gen51424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51425" type="x-p"/> The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, which was written at Laodicea in Pisidia, was sent by the hands of Tychicus. - Syriac. <div eID="gen51425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51426" type="x-p"/> The end of the Epistle; and it was written at Athens. - Arabic. <div eID="gen51426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51427" type="x-p"/> To the Thessalonians. - Aethiopic. <div eID="gen51427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51428" type="x-p"/> Written from Athens, and sent by Silvanus and Timotheus. - Coptic. <div eID="gen51428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51429" type="x-p"/> No subscription in the Vulgate. <div eID="gen51429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51430" type="x-p"/> Written at Corinth. - Author of the Synopsis. - sent by Titus and Onesimus. - Latin Prologue. <div eID="gen51430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51431" type="x-p"/> The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, written from Rome. - No. 71, a MS. of the Vatican library, written about the eleventh century. <div eID="gen51431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51432" type="x-p"/> The chief of the MSS. either have no subscription, or agree with some of the above versions. <div eID="gen51432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51433" type="x-p"/> That the epistle was neither written at Athens, Laodicea, nor Rome, has been sufficiently proved; and that it was written, as well as the first, at Corinth, is extremely probable. See the preface, and what has been said on the preceding epistle. <div eID="gen51433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51434" type="x-p"/> I have often had occasion to observe that the subscriptions at the end of the sacred books are not of Divine origin; they are generally false; and yet some have quoted them as making a part of the sacred test, and have adduced them in support of some favourite opinions. <div eID="gen51434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51435" type="x-p"/> Finished correcting this epistle for a new edition, the shortest day in 1831. - A.
