               <ns0:head>CHAP. III.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 FInally <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Apostle now draws towards the close of his Epistle, as appears by the word <ns0:hi>Finally,</ns0:hi> which he also useth in the close of other Epistles as 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.11. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.10. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.8. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. It imports the adding of something that remains.</ns0:note> brethren, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 4.3.</ns0:note> pray for us <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And that which he first addeth, is the desire of their Prayers, as he had desired them in the former Epistle, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 5. <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 25. And so of other Churches, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.11. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.19. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.18. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> He had prayed for them in the foregoing Chap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, and now he begs their Prayers. It is a mutual duty, that Ministers and People owe to one another; though the Apostle gave himself to the <ns0:hi>word, and prayer also, Acts</ns0:hi> 6.4. yet the Prayers of many may be more prevalent then of one, though an Apostle: And they being concerned for the advancing of Christs interest in the World, as they were Christians, were therefore ingaged to pray for him. And the Apostle was sen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sible of the greatness of the work which was in his hand, and his own insufficiency, without God, therefore he desires Prayer; and it is of them whom he here calls <ns0:hi>brethren</ns0:hi>; he knew the Prayers of the wicked and unbelievers would avail nothing; and though he was a great Apostle, yet the greatest in the Church may stand in need of, and be helped by the Prayers of the meanest Brethren.</ns0:note>, that the word of the Lord may have <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>free</ns0:hi> course <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">And their Prayers he desires are, first, with respect to his Ministry; <ns0:hi>That the word of the Lord may have free course,</ns0:hi> or may run; that the course of it may not be stopt, it being as a River of the water of Life. The Apostle was to teach all Nations, and so desires the word may pass from one Nation to another, yea, and run down from one Generati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on to another, that it may spread, and diffuse it self, and Disciples might be multiplyed. This is call'd the <ns0:hi>encreasing of it, Acts</ns0:hi> 6.7. <ns0:hi>The growing and multiplying of it, Acts</ns0:hi> 12.24. <ns0:hi>The growing and prevailing of it, Acts</ns0:hi> 19.20. Which Christ sets forth by the parable of the Mustard-seed, which grew and spread, and of the Leaven that diffused its vertue in the Meal, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 13.31, 32, 33. The Apostle referring here to the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternal course of the word, rather then its inward efficacy in the soul, as also Christ seems chiefly to do in those parables. There are many things that hinder the course of the Gospel, some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times wicked Rulers make Laws against it, sometimes great per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />secutions have been raised, sometimes false Teachers oppose it, sometimes Professors prove Apostates, and scandalize the world against it, sometimes reproaches are thrown in the way of it. And to the free course of it is required, on the contrary, a pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vision of suitable help herein, both of Magistracy and Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stry, and the bestowing of the Spirit, and the blessing of en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deavours used herein, All these are to be pray'd for, as the former to be pray'd against.</ns0:note>, and be glorified <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">He means that it might have honour, reputation, and high esteem in the world, and not lye under reproach. As the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> accounted it Heresie, and the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> foolishness: As its said of those <ns0:hi>Gentiles, Acts</ns0:hi> 13.48. they glorified the word of the Lord, by their honourable re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect to it, and joy in it: As also that it might produce glori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous effects in the World, in subduing people to God, and ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king men new creatures, and bringing them out of the Devils into Christs Kingdom, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> That it may evidence it self to be from Heaven, and the power of God to mens Salvation, and not an invention of man: To which we may add, that it may be honoured in the unblameable and exemplary walking of the Professors of it.</ns0:note>, even as <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> with you <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The glorious success of it with them, he had largely shewn before in both these Epistles; and he would have them pray for the like with others. Those that have felt the power of the Gospel themselves to their Conversion and Salvation, should pray that others may partake of it with them. Herein they shew their charity to men, and love to God, which the Apostle here puts them upon , as that which would be ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceptable to God; and the rather, because their own experi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence might teach them, what God was able to do for others. Or else the Apostle in these words sets forth these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians,</ns0:hi> as a pattern of the mighty success of the word: It had its free course, and was glorified among them. They received it as the word of God, and not of men. As if the Apostle should say, they that would know the glorious success of the word of the Lord, let them go to <ns0:hi>Thessalonica.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 15.31.</ns0:note> that we may be delivered from <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>absurd,</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />reasonable and wicked men <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Their prayers are here desired by the Apostle, with respect to their persons, which relates to the prayer desired before, with respect to the word. For the Apostle and his fellow La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bourers met with such men that did oppose them, and by that means were hindered in their work of the Ministry, and the free course of the word obstructed: What were these men? were they the persecuting <ns0:hi>Gentiles?</ns0:hi> They met with such, or the envious, malicious <ns0:hi>Iews?</ns0:hi> They met with such also; and here at <ns0:hi>Thessalonica</ns0:hi> in particular, and which followed <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Berea, Acts</ns0:hi> 17. Or were they false Brethren crept into the Church; as he complains of his perils by them, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.26. which some think most probable, by what he adds, for all men have not faith, even of those that make profession. Why may not we take in all these? but whoever they were, he stiles them, first, <ns0:hi>unreasonable men,</ns0:hi> men out of place, as the word im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ports; taken either literally for vagrants, wanderers, not keep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers at home: Or such as follow the Apostle from place to place, to hinder his Ministry. Or Logically, for men that argued ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />surdly, and kept to no sound Topics in reasoning. Either false Teachers among the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> or the Heathen Philosophers, such as he met with at <ns0:hi>Athens,</ns0:hi> whom he disputed with, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 17. Or Morally, for men that had corrupt Principles, and practises, that kept not to the duty of their place and station, <ns0:hi>Desordonnez French</ns0:hi> Translation, and wandred out of the path of Righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness. We render it <ns0:hi>unreasonable men</ns0:hi>; men transported with fury and passion against all reason, as we read of the <ns0:hi>Iews, Acts</ns0:hi> 17.5. Or such as acted contrary to reason, as the Apostle speaks of such Jews in the former Epistle, who were contrary to all men, <ns0:hi>forbidding them to preach to the Gentiles, that they might be saved,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 2.16. Or men of sensual lives, living more like brutes then reasonable creatures. Secondly, <ns0:hi>wicked men,</ns0:hi> so that whoever they were, whether <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi>; teachers or the common people, learned or unlearned, they were wicked, and whatever was meant by the former word, yet this is plain; and the word imports either men that are laborious in wickedness, or that by their wickedness create labour and trouble to others. And such the Apostle met with at <ns0:hi>Thessalonica, Iews</ns0:hi> who took to them <ns0:hi>certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and drew Iason and others before the rulers, assaulting his house, Acts</ns0:hi> 17.5. And in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed wherever they came, they met with such kind of men: Through the lusts of mens hearts, and the enmity and malice of the Devil, faithful Ministers will meet with opposition, and such as will hinder what they can the free course of the word. And therefore the Apostle desires prayer to be delivered from them, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, the word signifies a rescue by strength from some impending or incumbent evil, oft used, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 1.74. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.13. <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>ult.</ns0:hi> And he desires deliverance rather for the Gospels sake then his own. And though it is honourable to suffer for the Gospel, yet it is desireable to be kept out of the hands of such men as these.</ns0:note>, for all men have not faith <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The Apostle subjoyns the rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son why men are thus, for <ns0:hi>all men have not faith.</ns0:hi> He needed not say this of Infidels, which all men know to be without it, and therefore its thought the Apostle here means Professours. There may be true Faith wanting where Faith is professed. Faith is sometimes taken for fidelity, a moral vertue, and some think is meant here, because it follows in the next verse by way of Antithesis, <ns0:hi>but God is faithful:</ns0:hi> But rather, I take it for a Theological Grace. For that true Evangelical Faith which pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rifies the heart, and worketh by love, and brings forth the <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> of Obedience to all Gods Commandments. Had they this faith they would not be unreasonable and wicked? But can we sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose such to be in the Church? as well as those 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.5. whom the Apostle describes to have a form of Godliness under all that wickedness he there mentions. But let men have Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vility, Sobriety, External Devotion and Profession, yet if they oppose the Gospel, in the power, purity and progress of it, they may be stiled unreasonable and wicked men; and from such men we may pray, as the Apostle desired here, <ns0:hi>Good Lord deliver us.</ns0:hi> And it is the duty of people with respect to their faithful Ministers, and the work of the Gospel in their hands, to pray that they may be delivered from such men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Thes. 5.24.</ns0:note> the Lord is faithful, who shall establish you <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">These words are added by way of consolation; 1. With respect to their establishment, which the Apostle had before prayed for, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 17. and here he assures them of it, what God hath promised yet, we may and ought to pray for. And Ministers should exhort people to seek that grace which they may be sure before hand God will give: And this esta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blishment respects either their mind, in the belief of the gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel against false Doctrine, or their hearts against inordinate fears of men, or their practise, against departing from the way of Holiness. The Apostle well knew the <ns0:hi>Tenure</ns0:hi> of the New Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venant which contains promises of perseverance and establish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, as well as of pardoning Mercy, and sanctifying Grace, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>er. 32.40. And he grounds his confidence of their establish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment upon Gods faithfulness, as upon the same account he com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />forts the <ns0:hi>Corinthians,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.13. and these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Epist.</ns0:hi> 5.24. and it may be the Apostle hath here reference to what he had said before; though we shall meet with wicked and unreasonable men, yet fear not, God will establish you, for he is faithful. As Gods promises are according to his pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poses, so his performances will be according to his promises, which is his faithfulness.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 17.15.</ns0:note> keep <ns0:hi>you</ns0:hi> from evil <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">2. As God would establish them, so <ns0:hi>keep them from evil.</ns0:hi> There is moral and penal evil, of sin and suffering; the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word imports the former: Never used but for sinful evil, or sometimes for the Devil, with respect to the sin that dwells in him, and occasioned by him, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.16. 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.18. And its true, that God will keep his people from the Devil, as some read the word. But I suppose the Apostle means here by evil, <ns0:hi>evil work</ns0:hi>; as he speaks, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.18. <ns0:hi>God will preserve me from every evil work.</ns0:hi> But whether the evil work of others, or their own? the latter I incline to, for he could not well assure them of the former. But how could he assure them of the latter? did he think God would keep them from all sin? The Apostle doth not mean so, nor say so; God keeps his People from much evil and sin which others fall into though not from all. And he keeps them from falling under the power of it. Though they may be tempted by Satan, the World or their own hearts, yet not so as finally to be over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />come. However, the more God doth establish his People, the more will they be kept from evil. And the Apostle doth also comfort them in this from the consideration of Gods faithfulness. But these promises of Gods keeping us, do not exclude our en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deavours of keeping our selves. <ns0:hi>He that is born of God keepeth himself, and the wicked one toucheth him not,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.18. Hence those exhortations, <ns0:hi>Keep thy heart with all diligence, Prov.</ns0:hi> 4.23. and <ns0:hi>keep your selves in the love of God, Iude</ns0:hi> 21. <ns0:hi>&c..</ns0:hi> And our keeping is ascribed to our own faith with the power of God, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.5.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:528" />4 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 7.16.</ns0:note> we have confidence in the Lord touching you that ye both do, and will do the things that we command you <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Apostle had before declared his confidence that God would establish them and keep them from evil, and now here declares his confidence in them concerning their obedience. For he knew well that this is the way of Gods keeping men, and whereby he shews that he built his confidence concerning what he had before declared about their Election, Calling, E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stablishment and Preservation upon some good ground. And he describes their obedience by doing what the Apostle, and his Fellow-Labourers in the Gospel among them commanded them, whether they were Commandments about the duties of the Law of the first or second Tables, or the Doctrine, Order, Worship or Discipline of the Gospel. So that their Commandements were no other but the Commandements of the Lord himself, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 28.20. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.37. Ministers are not arbitrary Commanders in the Church. Not Lords over Gods Heritage, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.3. or have dominion over the peoples Faith, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.24. nor may they, as the Pharisee, teach for Doctrine the Commandments of men, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 15.9. And he speaks before of these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> that they received the word preached by them, not as the word of men but of God, 1 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 2.13. Both our Faith and Practice in Religion is, to be built upon Divine Authority. Either upon what God hath ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />presly declared, or what by clear Consequence may be derived from it. So that what they command the people is from the Lord, and not themselves. Their work is to search out the Mind and Will of Christ, as revealed in the Scripture, seeing they have not that immediate infallible inspiration that the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postles had, who were called to lay the foundation which others were to build upon. And as to those things that are but ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pendixes, and not of the substance of Religion, and for which no particular Rule is or can be laid down Christian prudence is to regulate them according to general Rules, wherein the advice, appointment and authority of the Minister is to be regarded in every Church. Yet nothing ought to be enjoyned in these things that is uncomly, that is not for edification, that is not of good report<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> that hath an appearance of Evil, that gives just oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion of offence, that transgresseth the general Rule of Mercy, that is a direction of superstition, whereby many of the Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandments of the <ns0:hi>Romish</ns0:hi> Church are justly condemned. And obedience to these Commandments of the Apostle he describes it by the universality of it, <ns0:hi>the things that we command you</ns0:hi>; that is all things; the indefinite being equivalent to the univer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sal. And by the constancy of it, that <ns0:hi>you both do, and will do, &c.</ns0:hi> ye will persevere to do what Comandments ye have already received, or any new Commmandments we shall further give you; some whereof are probably such as are mentioned in the following part of this Chapter. And their present obedience gave the Apostle confidence about that which was future. At least he declares to them this confidence, as an insinuating ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gument to perswade them thereunto.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Here the Apostle prays for them again, as he had done a little before, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2.17. and as this shews how much they were in his heart; so the frequent mingling of Prayers with his exhortations shews they could not be effectual without God. And he prayes for two things, 1. <ns0:hi>To have their hearts directed into the love of God</ns0:hi>; which is either meant passively for Gods love to them, to have their hearts, that is their whole Soul ingaged in the study, contemplation and admiration of this love; Or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther actively, for their love to God; to have their hearts set strait into the love of God, as the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word imports; drawn out towards him as a strait line to its Centre, or as an arrow directed to the mark. Till Mans love is set upon God, the mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions of the heart are crooked and irregular. As the wayes of sin are call'd crooked wayes, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 125.5. and <ns0:hi>Iohn Baptists</ns0:hi> Ministry was to make crooked things straight, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 40.4. The turning mans heart and wayes towards God makes them strait. <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> prays, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119.36. <ns0:hi>Incline my heart to thy testimonies</ns0:hi>; <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Or, <ns0:hi>bend my heart.</ns0:hi> As we bend a crooked stick to make it straight. Or as he he prays God to unite his heart to his fear, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 86.11. so here <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> to direct theirs to his love, by which some understand all Religion. We learn hence, that to direct mans heartto the love of God is the work of God, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />yond our power. And the hearts of the best Saints stand in need of a more perfect and constant direction unto the Love of God.</ns0:note>, and into the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>patience of Christ.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> patient waiting for Christ <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Patient sufferings for Christs sake; as the Apostle calls his sufferings for Christs sake, the sufferings of Christ often, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.5. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.10, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and patience for his sake, is call'd the patience of Christ, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 1.9. And the word is often used in this sence for pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tience under the Cross. And so the Apostle hath his eye in his Prayer upon the suffering state these Believers were in for Christs sake. If the sence be rendred as in our Translation, he prays for their hearts to be fixed upon the coming of Christ, to look towards it, and patiently to wait for it. The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word being often taken for the patience of expectation as well as of suffering, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.25. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.36. and so it is the same as <ns0:hi>waiting for the Son of God from Heaven,</ns0:hi> mentioned 1 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>last.</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>looking for the Saviour, Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.20. that hereby they might not faint under their sufferings, nor be surprized by his coming. And because the hearts of the best are apt either to be remiss or secure upon the delay of Christs coming, he therefore prays their hearts might be <ns0:hi>directed</ns0:hi> to a patient wait<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing for it, as the Apostle <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> upon the same account exhorts Believers to the girding up the Loyns of their Mind, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Here the Apostle proceeds to a discourse of another kind, which is about their carriage to disorderly Members in the Church. And having before declared his confidence, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 4. <ns0:hi>that they did, and would do the things he commanded them,</ns0:hi> he now tells them what he commands; and because either 'tis a matter of great importance, or that which they would be backward in, he therefore speaks with the greater vehemence, when he spake in the former Epistle, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 5.14. of warning the unruly, he then spake with greater mildness, <ns0:hi>We exhort you brethren,</ns0:hi> &c. but now to withdraw from them is an harsher Duty; or they having first warned them, if they reform not next, they are to proceed to withdraw from them. And this he now commands as that which he supposeth they might be backward to. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. The word properly signifies a command con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veighed from another, so the Apostle commands here in the Name of the Lord Jesus. Though he had Authority to com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand as an Apostle, yet it was derived to him from Christ, and therefore usually conjoyns Christ with his Exhortati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons and commands;</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 16.17. ver. 14. Joh. 10.2.</ns0:note> that you withdraw your selves from every brother <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">or to avoid as the word signifies, and is so rendred, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.20. The word is used also, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.12. of <ns0:hi>Peters</ns0:hi> withdrawing himself from eating with the Gentiles. And rendred drawing back, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.38. alluding as some think there to a Souldier that draws back from the Battel. But here in the Text to a Marriner that steers his ship from the rocks, and so it implies the danger of not withdrawing, which may be the reason of the Apostles so solemn command about it. And it is not from an Heathen man, but a <ns0:hi>Brother.</ns0:hi> One that is of the Church, and it is every Brother, let him be rich or poor, high, or low, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> As he writes to the <ns0:hi>Corinthi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.11. <ns0:hi>If any man that is call'd a Brother be a Fornica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tor,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>, that walketh <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Thes. 4.11. ver. 14. chap. 2.15.</ns0:note> disorderly, and not after the traditi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on he received of us <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Alluding as some think to Souldiers who keep not their rank, not walking according to rule, or, as he expresseth it, <ns0:hi>Not according to the tradition which he received of us.</ns0:hi> What is to be meant by Tradition, is explained in the former Chap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter. And he cannot be understood to speak here of Rites and Ceremonies relating to Church<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Worship, or Order, as some imagine. The Apostle doth in the following Verses explain himself otherwise. But what is this withdrawing? Is it <ns0:hi>Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />communication</ns0:hi> the greater or the less? In a general sence it may be so called, for it is an abstaining from Communion, but it is not so properly; for that is called <ns0:hi>putting away a person, a purg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing out the old leaven,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.7. this is only a withdrawing from him, much less is it a delivering up to Satan, which the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle required, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5. and himself inflicted upon <ns0:hi>Hymeneus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Alexander,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>last.</ns0:hi> The nature of the crime here mentio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned will not bear that. It was not Incest or Blasphemy, as in the former Instances, but only disorderly walking, which he specifies afterwards. And with respect to such the Apostle re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired in the former Epistle, warning only, <ns0:hi>warn the unruly.</ns0:hi> And though this is something more, yet it implies not a cast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing a man out of the Church, which is Christ's visible Kingdom into Satans Kingdom, for he is still to be admonisht as a Bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, as <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 15. And Excommunication is the exerting an Act of Church power, as 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.4. whereof no mention is made here, or of an absolute rejection which is elsewhere re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 3.10. It seems then to be only a withdrawing from familiar converse and society. As 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.11. <ns0:hi>If any man that is call'd a Brother be a Fornicator, Covetous, &c. with such an one no not to eat,</ns0:hi> alluding to the custom of the Jews who would not eat with the Gentiles, and by eating is exprest Communion in Scripture, and prophane Writers also. And such Communion is forbidden to such a brother, which the Apostle allowed them to have with such sinners that were of the World, and not of the Church, as <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 10. which cannot be meant of sacred communion. And familiarity with such a brother would harden him in his sins, and reflect dishonour up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on Religion, and indanger their infection more than with a <ns0:hi>Pagan,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Infidel</ns0:hi>; which therefore the Apostle forbids them to a Brother. As he did the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> mentioned before, as also the <ns0:hi>Romans, chap.</ns0:hi> 16.17. And which may be a step towards excommunication from Spiritual communion; which is the greater punishment, especially if the brother be not hereby made ashamed, and reform his course, and doth not only now and then do a disorderly action, but <ns0:hi>walks disorderly</ns0:hi> and that after warning also. Others think its meant of Excom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />munication, and judg not the reason against it to be cogent.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="10">10 For <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The words contain a reason, as the illative <ns0:hi>for,</ns0:hi> imports, but what it refers to is uncertain, most probably a further rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son of the Apostles working with his hands, because when with them he left this command, <ns0:hi>that he that would not work should not eat</ns0:hi>; he would therefore practise himself what he command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed them, and not be thought to be as the <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> binding heavy burdens upon others, and he not touch them himself.</ns0:note> even when we were with you, this we commanded you <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">And this is another of the Commandments which the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle gave them, which he declared his confidence that they would do, <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 4. and this command seems grounded upon the law given to <ns0:hi>Adam, In the sweat of thy brows thou shalt eat bread, Gen.</ns0:hi> 3.19.                      <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 6. And now he lays his Commandment upon them<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="4 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>es, and that in the name of Christ.</ns0:note>, that with quietness they work <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Working is set opposite to their idleness, and quietness to their busie medling where they ought not, whereby they might occasion strife. The Apostle here, and in many other places requires Christians to live peaceably, as 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.11. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.15. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.13. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.14.</ns0:note>, and eat their own bread <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Not to live as drones upon o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers labours, yet he forbids not dealing their bread to the hun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gry; nor requires this of the poor that are necessitated to live upon alms: And by eating their own bread the Apostle means, maintaining themselves, and Families, for bread is taken in Scripture for all things that maintain the natural Life: And the Apostle here insinuates a blessing upon honest labour, that thereby men shall have bread of their own: and doth assert property against that community which some have pleaded for, the civil right that men have to what they honestly get and pos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sess, but hereby condemn Oppressours, Pirats, Robbers, Cheat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers, Usurpers, yea, and Tyrannical Princes, who maintain them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves upon the spoil of others, and take their bread out of o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers mouths: And why not also such as are not quiet and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tented with their own portion, but either envy others, or mur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mure against providence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 But ye, brethren <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle now directs his speech to those of the Church, that were not guilty of the disorders before mentioned, to whom he speaks in mild and familiar Language, as if the others deserved not to be so called.</ns0:note>, be not <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>faint not.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> weary in well doing <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">And that which he speaks to them is, <ns0:hi>not to be weary of well-doing.</ns0:hi> The Greek word is often used about sufferings, as 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.1. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 3.13. and then usu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally Translated <ns0:hi>fainting,</ns0:hi> and which seems to be its most proper use, to shrink or faint as cowards in War, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>Ne segnescite, desmite, desatigamini,</ns0:hi> it signifies a receding or fainting, or tiring in our duty, because of the evil that attends it, some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times its used of prayer, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 18.1. and sometimes generally of all duties of Religion, which are generally call'd well doing, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.9. and signifies either a slothfulness in them, or weari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of them; as those whom the Prophets complain of, <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 8.5. <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 1.13. the Apostle useth the same word in this sence, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.9. <ns0:hi>Be not weary of well-doing</ns0:hi>; and in the Text, those that did walk orderly, he exhorts them to hold on their course, either more peculiarly to the works of Charity, which are called well-doing, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.14. Though those that workt not did not deserve them, or enjoy them, yet this should not discourage them from practising them towards others; or the word may extend more generally to all good works, we should persevere in them without fainting or weariness, notwithstand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />ing the evils that may threaten us therein.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And if any man obey not our word <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>signifie that man by an Epistle.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, by this epistle <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Here we have further Commandments given concerning the disorderly. In case of obstinacy to proceed further against them. The Apostle had given Commandments about their walking in his first preaching to them, after that he repeats them in his first Epistle, and again in this second. And now if any man obey not our word by this Epistle, saith he, <ns0:hi>note that man,</ns0:hi> and he would have none excepted, either through fear or favour, and nothing done by partiality. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 5.21.</ns0:note>, note that man <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">What is meant by <ns0:hi>noting</ns0:hi> is disputed among expositors, more seems to be meant then <ns0:hi>marking them, Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.17. Some take it for what we call Excommunication, so <ns0:hi>Aug. lib.</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>Cont. Epist. Parmen. cap.</ns0:hi> 4. <ns0:hi>Theophyl. in locum,</ns0:hi> either the casting him out of the Church, which is the greater, or suspension from the Lords Supper, which is the lesser. As there were degrees of Church censure among the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> so also we read practised in the Gospel Church, as is evident in the Councils. Others think it is no more than a withdrawing from him, as was men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned before, <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 6. but then the Apostle saith the same thing over again, which seemeth needless. And he speaks here of some greater contumacy then before, when his word in this se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cond Epistle is not obeyed. We may suppose the Apostle may mean not only a withdrawing from familiarity with him, but exposing his name to some publick notice in the Church, that both his crime and his name should be publickly noticed. As the Apostle speaks of <ns0:hi>Hymeneus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Alexander,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Philetus,</ns0:hi> by name in his Epistles that were made publick. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
Note him by a sign, as the word signifies, which cannot well be done by a meer withdrawing. And seeing he speaks here of one that is not only disorderly, but obstinate, some further and more signal act of Discipline is to be inflicted on him, And what word the Apostle refers to in this Epistle as not obeyed, is not exprest, neither need we limit it, but may be meant of all his Commandments herein, to which obedience was required. And the word, as written, is the word of God, and is to be obeyed as well as that which is preached. I know there is ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther reading of the Text, <ns0:hi>If any man obey not our word, note that man by an Epistle,</ns0:hi> and so it is in our Margins. But this is not probable; by an Epistle? to whom? To the Apostle himself? And for what? to know how to procede towards such an one? What need that when he here gives direction about it to them: which follows,</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 5.9, 11. ver. 6.</ns0:note> have no company with him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or be not mingled with him, which refers either to his crime as the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word is so applyed, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5.11. or to his person also, as the word is used, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.9. And yet some think the Apostle here forbids only Civil Communion, not Sacred, because the word in the Text is generally so used, and so rendred by Expositors, but Sacred Communion is exprest in the new Testament by another word, 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.3. And if meant of Sacred, it is then casting him out of the Church, which is a delivering him up to Satan, <ns0:hi>Vid. Estius in loc.</ns0:hi> And that seems not to agree with what follows, <ns0:hi>Admonish him as a Brother</ns0:hi>: and so not to be ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />counted as an Heathen or a Publican, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 18.17. And we know admonition goes before casting out. But to be thrust out of the company of the people of God in all Civil Friendly Society is a great punishment and affliction. And some think that the <ns0:hi>noting</ns0:hi> of him was to be done by the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vernours of the Church, and the renouncing his Company by all the people, let the reader judge.</ns0:note>, that he may be a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shamed <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The end of both is here exprest. This is not added before as a reason of with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />drawing, and therefore some think the Apostle required that only to avoid the Infection of sin by familiar society; but this further proceeding here mentioned is to make the man ashamed that is obstinate in disobedience, but we need not so limit it. <ns0:hi>And this making him ashamed</ns0:hi> is not to be out of hatred to his person, but for his good, as all Church censures ought to be so intended, to bring him to that shame that may be the first step to true Repentance. There is a shamefulness in sin; and when sinners repent, they see it, and are ashamed, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 1.29. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 16.61, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.21. And God complains of sinners when not ashamed, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 3.3. Shame is a natural affection in men, and is not in the nature of Beasts, neither was it in man before the fall; and though in its self it is no vertue, being the proper effect of sin, yet it is of use to restrain much open wicked<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, and to keep decorum in mens outward actions: And God makes use of it also in leading men to true Repentance. To shame men out of envy or hatred is sinful; and against the Law of Charity, but to do it to bring them to Repentance, is better than by flattery or familiar Society to harden them in sin.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Yet count <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> not as an enemy <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">They having thus proceeded against the disorderly and disobedient, the Apostle directs them about their after carriage, which either respects their inward opinion of the mind, or out<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward action. They should not <ns0:hi>count him an Enemy,</ns0:hi> putting a great difference betwixt an offending Brother, and a professed Enemy. They ought not to hate him as an Enemy, not look up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on him as upon such who out of enmity to the Gospel persecute Christianity, nor to have an unreconcileable mind towards him.</ns0:note>, but ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monish <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> as a brother <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">And as to outward action, should admonish him as a Brother. It is either private or publick, Ministerial or Fraternal, gentle, or severe, joyn'd with commination. The Greeks express it in the degrees of it by three words, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. The word in the Text signifies a putting in mind. They were to put the offender in mind of his sin, and in mind of his duty. Though they were to have no company with him, in a way of familiarity, yet to be in his company, so as to admonish him; and the admonition here meant is either publick, in the Church, or private, or first private then publick, as our Saviour gives the rule, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 18.17. So that his Repentance is to be endea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />voured, not only by abstaining his company, but by admoni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion. And it is to be performed to him <ns0:hi>as a brother,</ns0:hi> which ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther respects the state of the person admonisht. He is not an Enemy, or Pagan, or one out of the visible Church, but a Bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, whereby some conceive that the Apostle had not before spoken of his Excommunication. Or it respects the way of ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monition. It is to be performed with love, tenderness and com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />passion, as to a brother, not to upbraid him, but to gain him, as <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 18.15. <ns0:hi>If he hear thee thou hast gained thy brother.</ns0:hi> And for that end great prudence is to be used. The temper of the offenders, the quality of the sin, their outward condition in the world, their age, yea, the circumstances of time and place are to be considered.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Now <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 15.33</ns0:note> the Lord of peace himself give you peace <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Apostle is now taking his leave, and closing up his E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pistle; and this he doth with prayer, and what he prays for is peace, and though the word peace hath various acceptions, and is of comprehensive signification, yet here it is to be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood of brotherly peace and unity: Whether it was occa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion'd by any dissensions that were actually among them, or his fears of such to arise upon the practise of their duties to the disorderly among them that he thus prayes, is uncertain; and it is that which he much presseth and prayes for in his several Epistles to the Churches, as being that wherein the honour of the Gospel, and their own comfort and edification, were so much concerned: And the person he prays to, he stiles the <ns0:hi>Lord of Peace,</ns0:hi> whereby I suppose he means Jesus Christ, who is sometimes called the <ns0:hi>Prince of peace, Isa.</ns0:hi> 9.6. As God is called the <ns0:hi>God of Peace,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.23. It is he that hath made peace betwixt God and us, betwixt the Jew and Gentile, and it is one of the fruits of his Spirit in the hearts of Christians, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.22. True Christian peace is the gift of Christ, and therefore the Apostle prays the Lord to give it, and saith, the <ns0:hi>Lord himself,</ns0:hi> as intimating none but he can give it, and that it is a singular blessing to enjoy it, as we must so interpret the phrase when at any other time we find it, as 1 <ns0:hi>Thessonians</ns0:hi> 5.23.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>every where</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>in every <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> alwayes, by all means <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He shews both the desirableness and difficulty of peace. It is worth the using all endeavours for it, and without such we shall hardly attain it, as <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.18. <ns0:hi>If it be possible, as much as lyeth in you, live peaceably with all men,</ns0:hi> Quite contrary to the temper and practise of some men, who will live peaceably with no man; and elsewhere we read of <ns0:hi>following Peace, Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.14. and <ns0:hi>seeking peace and ensuing it,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.11. and <ns0:hi>endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of Peace, Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.3. And the Apostle prays for it in the Text with much earnestness, and that they might enjoy it without interruption, <ns0:hi>alwayes.</ns0:hi> That there might be no schisme rise up among them at any time, and if we read the next words <ns0:hi>in every thing,</ns0:hi> he prays that their peace might be universal with respect to opini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons, words and actions, and as a final farewell addeth, <ns0:hi>the Lord be with you all,</ns0:hi> which shews his affection to them all, though he had reproved sharply the disorders that some were guilty of. And a greater thing he could not desire for them. It compre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hends all blessings in it, and the very blessedness of heaven it self. As a usual farewell word <ns0:hi>Adieu</ns0:hi> is a recommending a per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son to God.</ns0:note>. The Lord <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> with you all.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:529" />17 The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This the Apostle addeth after he had finisht his Epistle, and taken his farewel, as a proof that the Epistle was genuine, and came from himself. Because it may be there were some then who did counterfeit his Epistles, as there have been many since who have counterfeited Creeds, Liturgies, Gospels, Writ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings of the Fathers, &c. and he knew it might be of dangerous consequence to the Churches, to have his Writings counter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feited. Hereticks in several Ages, and the Church of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> particularly hath herein been deeply guilty. And though its probable the body of this Epistle was Writ by some <ns0:hi>Amanuensis,</ns0:hi> as is evident of the Epistle to the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> that it was writ by one <ns0:hi>Tertius, Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.22. and when he tels the <ns0:hi>Galatians, Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.11. he wrote their Epistle with his own hand, so <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 1.9. it implies sometimes he did not so. Yet this Salutation he wrote with his own hand, which he practised not only in this, but in all his other Epistles, as he here affirmed. And he wrote it in such characters whereby his own hand might be known. Else it was an easie matter for any impostor to write the same words, and the words of it are here set down, but elsewhere explained, and therefore nothing is further needful here.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> with you all. Amen.</ns0:p>
